title: Some computer clocks will overflow on 19 January 2038
body: Much software counts time as seconds since 1 January 1970. Stored as a signed 32-bit number, that count tops out at 2,147,483,647, which falls at 03:14:07 UTC on 19 January 2038. One second later it wraps to a negative number, which affected systems read as a date in December 1901. Most modern systems already use 64-bit time, but old embedded devices and file formats may still be at risk.

slides.prompt: When the 32-bit counter wraps, what date do affected systems think it is?
slides.detail: One second after 03:14:07 UTC the signed count flips to a negative number, which reads as a date in 1901. Most modern systems already use 64-bit time.

slides.heading: What a 32-bit clock can count
slides.note: A signed 32-bit count of seconds reaches 2,147,483,647 at 03:14:07 UTC on 19 January 2038.

slides.clue: What happens when a count passes the largest value its bits can hold and wraps around
slides.detail: One second after 03:14:07 UTC on 19 January 2038, a signed 32-bit second counter flips negative.
